utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis. We are assisted today by our intern Lisa Hartog and our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Defence? Mr. Registrar, what are we going to do about this noise?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good morning to everyone, but I'm afraid we can't go on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be working now. The Chamber bids good morning to all those present. I didn't have time to say this because we were having technical difficulties. Good morning to the Prosecution, counsel, and the accused, as well as all the personnel of this courtroom, without forgetting the interpreters who are behind the walls. In view of the fact that we had this problem, I would like to ask the registrar that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence counsel now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I start examining the witness, I think it would be customary to give the witness a sheet of paper on which he will note down his name, family name, and his initials HB. This document will later be sealed. This is in order to know the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will have a look at the document. Could you also write down the date. It's the 30th of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Show the date to the Defence, and to Mr. Mundis, too. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number will be DH349, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may proceed, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness HB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session again as I want to ask the witness some questions that relate to his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can't see the little logo anymore, so we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, tell me, where were you when the JNA and the Serbian army attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever leave Banja Luka, and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I left Banja Luka around October 1992. I was in the prison in Banja Luka before that. The authorities at the time in Banja Luka had imprisoned me because allegedly I didn't have a permit to move around freely. And so I spent some time in the prison in the former police station in Banja Luka, and then in the Kozara barracks. Finally I went to Rakovacka Bara. That was a collection centre where they sent people to the army. Some captain released me there and gave me 24 hours to leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, did you leave Banja Luka within 24 hours? If not, why not? Or rather, did you leave Banja Luka at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't leave Banja Luka within 24 hours because it was impossible to do so. I had problems with my health, as I had been beaten up. I was bleeding. And it was necessary to obtain a lot of permits. But I left Banja Luka three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Banja Luka by bus. I went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay in Zagreb, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zagreb, the authorities that were receiving refugees in Croatia received me. As they saw that I had problems with my health, they placed me in the hospital where there were wounded Bosnians from the war. It was in the building of the tobacco factory Sarajevo. But I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question already put to you, Mr. HB, you said that sometime in October you went to Bosnia again. Who did you go to Bosnia with, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told the people in the hospital that I wanted to go to Bosnia because I considered myself a patriot. And there was an organised convoy Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond consisting of a number of buses that was going there. I was put on a bus together with combatants, HVO combatants from Doboj, from the Kotorsko village. I was in the bus with them. I didn't know where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, did you arrive in Zenica, and did you stay on in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I arrived in Zenica. The buses arrived there. We stayed in Zenica for one day. The soldiers were part of the Doboj corps, and they were going to Tesanj to find accommodation there. They asked me to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you accept their invitation? Who did you join? And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I accepted an invitation. Because I had arrived in Bosnia, I didn't know anyone. I got to know them on that trip to a certain extent. I went to Tesanj with them and became a member of the 203rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you a member of the brigade? Did you leave it, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was a member of the brigade up until about mid-January 1993. Then there was some sort of an announcement, according to which all the people from Krajina were to gather in Travnik and organise themselves to form a Krajina or Banja Luka Brigade. I received permission from the commander to leave, and I said I wanted to join up. I reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Travnik, and when, if you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I arrived in Travnik in mid-January, but when I arrived there, this so-called Banja Luka Brigade, well, it came to nothing. There weren't enough men. So the Territorial Defence sent me to Mehurici, where this brigade should have organised itself, since there was a unit in Mehurici at the time, near Banja Luka, Siprage, Kotor Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you find that unit there, which was mainly composed of men from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that's where I joined them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which brigade was that unit from Mehurici a part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit was part of the 306th Brigade; it was the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the headquarters of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade when you first arrived in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mehurici. That's where the headquarters of the 1st Battalion were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the soldiers and the command billeted? Do you remember which building you were billeted in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally. I spent a lot of time there. It was the only primary school in Mehurici. That's where the command was and that's where the unit was, at least the units that had arrived from Kotor Vares, Siprage, Mrkovici. It was fairly mixed. The compensation of the unit was fairly mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time were you assigned any duties, and if so, what kind of duties were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a certain period of time, I became the commander of the military police within that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior in the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the chief of security. His name was Hasan Zukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, how many of you were there in the military police unit at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, there were between eight and ten of us. But sometimes when we had a lot of work to carry out, older combatants from units from Siprage and Kotor Vares, et cetera, would come to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that older -- when you refer to older combatants, are you referring to their age, and if so, how old were these men who, in certain situations, joined your military police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to their age. On the whole, these men were about 50 years old, or over 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of tasks did your military police unit have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, its main tasks were as follows: We had to investigate errors made by combatants; we had to guard the command; and we had to carry out investigations if, for example, men left the lines, abandoned their positions, sold weapons. In some cases, they would even steal the livestock that belonged to the inhabitants. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, what sort of measures were taken against soldiers who violated the rules, or rather, who behaved in the manner that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we discovered that someone had violated the rules, we would take, on the whole, disciplinary measures. At the time we could only take disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you found out that a crime had been committed, what sort of authority did the police, or rather, the security organ have? What should you have done in such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if someone had committed a crime, then we would send a record of the event to the command, to the CSB and the brigade command. And they would then take further action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Against whom could you take measures, or rather, who did you investigate? Over whom did your military police have authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the military police was responsible only for army members. We would only carry out investigations into army members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, if certain offences were committed at the time by individuals who were not army members, in such cases, who would investigate these offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the civilian police would conduct the investigations into such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the time, in Mehurici, the civilian police was present, and do you know how many men it had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know the military police was near the school, and there were some professional policemen. I think they were policemen before the war, too. And they had some men from the so-called reserve police force who worked with them. We were on good terms. We even cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, when you arrived in the school in mid-January 1993, as you said, were there any other individuals staying in the school who were not members of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I arrived there, when I arrived in the school in Mehurici, there were only members of the 306th Brigade staying there. On the whole, they were from Kotor Vares and Siprage, Mrkonjic Grad; there were a few men from Jajce, and so on. This is where the police were -- this is where the men were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mehurici, and while staying in Mehurici, did you notice the presence of foreigners in Mehurici, specially foreigners from Afro-Asian countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would see them every day. They would pass by in cars. I would see them; they were present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were? Do you know where they had come from? And what do you call them at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, they looked like Arabs. It seems as if they were from Arab countries. They spoke a different language. The people called them Mujahedin, and I think that was an appropriate name for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mehurici, where were they staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were staying on a hill above Mehurici, about 200 to 300 metres away. On a hill, there's a place there where they had some sort of a camp up there, but I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that place, where they set up that camp, was that place secured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was some sort of a wire fence. There were some sort of guards up there, too. And it was only later, when there was an incident of some kind, that I noticed that there was some kind of a hedge Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond around the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, was it possible to gain free access to the camp, or rather, do you know whether men from your battalion and brigade had access to that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't think that there were any of us who knew what was happening in the camp, nor did any of us ever approach the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the 1st Battalion of the 306th, do you know whether these foreigners, these Mujahedin, trained men from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they provide you with logistic support? Did they provide you with food, weapons, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you notice that these foreigners were establishing relations with some of the population in Mehurici and its surroundings, and were there any Bosnians who joined these Mujahedin and stayed in the camp with them or cooperated with them in some other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were such people. The situation in the village was divided, because there were members of that unit who were from the village. And let me explain something. There was a mosque where the Mujahedin organised prayers or something like that. I don't know what they're called, but they organised an event. They had children going to the mosque, and they would instruct the children there. And I heard this, and I was also present on such an occasion. I heard that some of the older Mujahedin would marry young girls, 13- or 14-year-old girls.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, thank you. I would like to talk about the event that you referred to when answering one of my questions. Where were you at the beginning of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of June, I was in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you know what the situation was like in the Bila valley and in your brigade at the time? Were there any problems as far as relations with the HVO are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, perhaps at the end of May, the relations between the BH army and the HVO were very tense. I don't know the exact dates, but I can remember certain events. Our villages and the surroundings had been encircled. And on several occasions we received requests for assistance. We received requests to assist a village that had been attacked. I think the name of the village was Bukovica. I can't remember the name of these places very well now, but I think the name of the village was Bukovica. They asked for assistance, but our unit had been broken up. There weren't enough men. Some men couldn't return because the roads had been closed; there were blockades. And at that point in time, we couldn't provide any assistance. And the brigade command was also dispersed. It was in two or three places. So the situation was a bit chaotic, and it wasn't possible to organise ourselves in the way we should have been organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, nevertheless, at some point in time, did fighting break out, and could you tell us where you were on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know whether this happened on the 8th of June, but fighting did break out. We weren't able to help Bukovica because we believed that there were a lot of HVO troops up there. And I think that the command issued an order or decided to break through in the direction of Maline and Guca Gora. And it was then decided to carry out this breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, did you set off to carry out this breakthrough with the units in the morning, and if not, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't participant in this attempt to penetrate the lines. The command gave me a task as a member of the military police. They said that if they were to managed to penetrate the lines, the military police was to protect the civilians and the civilian population to try to establish some sort of order in the villages that we took or liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive an assignment at some point in time to leave Mehurici, and where were you told to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was told to go to Maline, because we had already heard that our troops had broken through the defence lines, that they had entered, and they had to go towards Guca Gora. So our assignment was to assist in the evacuation, or to assist the civilians who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, Mr. HB, when, roughly, this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got there while the fighting was still continuing, but I know that it was about 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning when we reached the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who did you find in the village once you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in the village, about midway, we came across our soldiers. There was still some shooting, but in the center, in the middle of the village, we found quite a large group of people who had gathered, as well as several members of the HVO who had surrendered. They were simply waiting there, and the troops were waiting for the police to arrive to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many of you military policemen arrived at the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 of us, because many others who were our members had left. We were short of men so that there were about 10 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. HB, what did you do when you saw this group of villagers and members of the HVO who had surrendered and who were standing in the center of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many civilians - women, children, old people - as well as a number of HVO members who had surrendered. The people were scared; they didn't know what to do, and they were afraid of something. It was difficult to explain and to make a decision in such a situation. People were coming out of their houses. There was even a woman who was wounded, and there were people who could not be moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone make a suggestion, who was it, and how did these people organise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As it was hard to explain things, because there was shooting, the people were crying, the women were crying, they didn't know what to do, they didn't dare stay in their homes, and I suggested that I take them all because I thought I could put them up in the school in Mehurici where they would be protected. And then the police would make sure that their property was intact and that nobody looted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people who had gathered in the center of the village, how did they react to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were different reactions. Some were in favour of going to Mehurici; others were against it. They didn't want to leave behind their homes, their property, their sick members. Some of them were bedridden; some were elderly, that couldn't walk. So the solution we found was to try and assist the older people and transport them to Mehurici by truck, including a wounded woman who was pregnant, she was transported by truck, whereas the others were to go on foot to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Mehurici from Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't be precise, especially after so much time. But if you took the road and you went by car, I think it would be about 13 or 14 kilometres. But if we used the path that we took, it was about 5 or 6 kilometres; that would be my rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the length of the route the only reason why you decided to take a shortcut instead of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The length of the road was one reason, because it's difficult to walk such a distance. However, there was fighting still going on in the valley. We didn't know who we could come across. There were very few of us escorting them. And the lines that our troops had broken through and that had been held by the HVO around the village were mined, so that the route we took to Mehurici was, in my view, the simplest for all of us to reach Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you took a shortcut, tell me, how did those people move? What was the formation? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a column. People went freely, three or four in a row. I'm not quite sure, but I think that there were three boxes of hand grenades that we had found in the village, and the HVO members who had surrendered, the prisoners of war, were carrying those boxes, two each. Otherwise, the women, children, and the elderly moved in rows of three or four.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many of you policemen went with those people to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, apart from me, there was another five policemen. I left the rest of them down there to take care of the houses and the property, to look after it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, Mr. HB, when it was that you set out towards Mehurici from Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could have been about 2.00 or 2.30 or 3.00 in the afternoon. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told me how those people were moving, but could you give an estimate, how many locals there were in addition to the HVO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, about 200 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, did you reach Mehurici without any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't. As we were moving along this path with the column, we were chatting. I would call it a friendly column. We were talking about why all this had happened, that it was a fine country before the war; was it the politicians who were to blame for all this. And, I don't know, it may have been about a kilometre before we reached Mehurici, from a thicket, two masked men jumped out. They demanded that I stop, and they said that they would take over the column. I told them that that was not possible, that we were members of the army and that we were taking the column to Mehurici, to the school there, where I thought they would probably be exchanged for some of our people held by the HVO, and that this would probably be resolved by the Red Cross. No, they demanded that they take them over straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, apart from those two men, during this conversation, did you notice anyone else arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five or six metres behind these two men were three Mujahedin. But later, when we were really quarrelling quite loudly, they cocked their guns and so I did the same. I don't know whether I was brave or a fool, I don't know, I really don't know. I thought that somehow we would resolve it. Then, from the wood, quite a number of men jumped out with their weapons pointed at us. All of them had some kind of hoods over their faces. And they said that they would kill us all. Whether we give them those people or not, they would kill us all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they cocked their guns. How did they do that with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these others had jumped out, this tall man, who demanded I surrender the people, he put his automatic rifle into my mouth and told me to drop my weapon. When I turned my head around, I saw that the others were pointing their guns at everyone, and one of them was pointing his gun at my brother, who was also a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this reaction on the part of the Mujahedin and the masked men, did you have any chance of resisting or surviving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I dropped my gun. And the people to the side, I couldn't really see everybody, but they took those people who were carrying the boxes. I don't know how many people they took. Maybe 15, maybe even 20, I don't know. But this was very brief. They just ran into the column, seized some men, and then they went off and let us pass. Everyone was terrified. I was scared and furious. And I ordered that we run as we were passing by the camp, and all of us ran to reach Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached Mehurici, where did you go with those people you had escorted to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first entered the school yard, and then from the yard, in a column, through the corridor, they all went to the sports hall of the elementary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's retrace our steps a little. When you said that they had put -- that one of the men had put his rifle into your mouth, were you hurt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, but not very seriously. They just cut my lip from the barrel of the gun, so I bled a little. But it's not really worth mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back again to the time when you left Maline. You said that at first, there were some people who were saying they wanted to go and others who found it hard to leave their homes. At the end, when you moved out, did everyone agree to move, or did you force some people to move with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All those who left, left by agreement, because many who didn't want to leave just then, their main reason was that they had somebody old or sick in the family whom they would have to leave. And when we managed to get hold of a truck going to Mehurici, I think five or six old people were evacuated by truck, and a pregnant woman, who was also wounded, she was also evacuated to Mehurici. And that was when the rest of the people all moved out with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you reached Maline around 9.00 or 10.00, that you were informed at 9.00 so you got there at about 10, and that you left sometime in the afternoon; you're not sure whether it was 1.00 or 2.00. What happened in the meantime in Maline itself? Did you spend all that time in discussion, or were there any other activities by the military police, preparing the population to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a small village. It is quite a large village. And having 10 men in the police, it's hard to tell who one could come across. There were soldiers. People were mixed. There was shooting on all sides. And we took care, if we came across a wounded man or somebody, we feared for our own lives, but we assisted. If there were wounded and sick, we tried to prevent any looting or any inappropriate treatment of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Maline, did you come across a lady doctor and some wounded people, or had they already left Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reached Maline, I didn't find them there. But this lady doctor is someone I met later at the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the first two jumped in front of you behind whom there were three Mujahedin, as you explained, these people who spoke to you, were they speaking in their own name or on behalf of the Mujahedin who were with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were speaking in the plural, and I quote: "We will now take over the care of these people." So this means in the plural, "we." And these two men, this tall one who put his gun in my mouth, he spoke Bosnian or Serbo-Croatian, our language anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were gathering the population in Maline, did you notice that the houses had been destroyed, or did you see anyone setting fire to those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. While we were there, no one did that. There were some houses that had been hit, in the operations perhaps, but there was no torching by soldiers. There was only a few houses from which smoke was coming, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's half past 10.00. We're going to have our technical break, and we will resume work around five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, before the break, you said that the population from Maline was placed in the primary school, you placed them in the primary school. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Did you provide them with anything to enable them to have accommodation in that sports hall in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived in the school, there were some mattresses -- some mats, rather, that were in the school, and from the place in which -- in the place where I slept, and other policemen, we had some mats and some blankets which we provided them with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone make a list of the people who had arrived then who were placed in the sports hall, and if so, what did you do with that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I personally made a list of all the people who were there, and I provided the command with this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, tell me, after their arrival, did anyone come to see these people immediately, and if so, who came to see them? And were any measures taken to provide these citizens with care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the evening, Dr. Ribic came; I think that was his name, or perhaps it was his nickname. He spoke to the lady doctor who was there, for the most part. I don't know what her name was. But he offered all the help he could offer, all the help they needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were women, children, and elderly people. Did anyone try to provide these people with food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know in what way. That evening, as night was falling, I don't know whether the inhabitants noticed them as we were passing through the village, or whether this was organised by someone from the civilian protection, but the inhabitants would bring what they had. Some of them would bring some pie; some of them would bring some cheese, et cetera. They provided them with some food. And the people who were in the school, the Croats, they had all brought some food with them. They had some food of their own with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When these people were brought to the primary school, did you inform anyone about what had happened on your way to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That very same night, my superior, the chief of security, well, he wasn't there, and none of the members of the command were there. They were at the forward command post. There was ongoing fighting. And it was only at dusk, when they had returned, that I provided the commander with a report. I think his name was Mrsa, but there was someone else called Fazlic there. I don't know what Mrsa's family name is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell those people that Mujahedin and masked men had intercepted you and had taken some of the people from the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to tell them anything at the time because I really was concerned with the fighting, et cetera, and I was waiting for my superior to arrive. And he did, in fact, arrive two days after the incident. I told him about everything in great detail, and I provided him with a report. This is what all the policemen in that group also did. He was provided a report on everything that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, on the basis of what you had said, your superior's name was Zukanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he carried out a detailed investigation, and did you provide written reports -- did you all provide written reports on what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was an investigation. We all gave written statements, which we left with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As someone who was responsible for taking the people there in safety, in a secure manner, how did you feel, given what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How did I feel? Well, it was difficult for me. I kept wondering whether I was responsible for everything that had happened, and I kept asking myself what the purpose of war was, what was the purpose of that war, since we Bosnians had no rights in our own country.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, on that day, on the first day, did you know anything about what had happened to those people, apart from the fact that they had been taken from the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about them. But on the following day, I went to replace the policeman who had stayed over in Maline that night. And when we returned to Mehurici, I found out that a group of our soldiers had brought a wounded HVO member, and he was also placed in the hall in Mehurici. I entered the hall because I wanted to see how badly he was wounded, I wanted to see why he had been wounded, and I wanted to register him. I think his name was Zeljko. And I recognised one of the men from the group taken away by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to him, Mr. HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I approached him. He was afraid. I don't know whether you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was afraid. The doctor who was dressing his wounds was there at that time. I asked him about what had happened, and he said that he managed to survive the execution. And I said, because at the time everyone would turn up, the Red Cross was supposed to turn up too, but at the time I didn't trust anyone. And I told him that it would be better for him to remain silent while he was there. That it would be better for him not to speak about that to anyone, not to tell anyone that he had survived the execution. I told him that once he was exchanged, he could then open up and say whatever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, since this is what you suggested to the wounded man you saw, the man who told you how he had been wounded, could you tell me why you made this suggestion? Was it because of your meeting with the Mujahedin, or was there some other reason for which you felt that something might happen if it was discovered that he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after that meeting, that close encounter, as I call it, with the Mujahedin, there was fighting. If there had been a full unit from the army in the school, perhaps I wouldn't have made such a suggestion. But since the unit was engaged in combat and there were only a few of us there in the school, if they had descended and come down from the hill -- well, this is what was on my mind at the time, perhaps my assessment was erroneous, but at the time I believed that it was best that that be kept secret, and I thought it would be best for them not to speak about what had happened until they were exchanged. To this very day, I'm not sure whether I was right or not in making this suggestion. But if the Mujahedin had found out about what the situation was, all of them would have probably been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, you said that a doctor came and provided them with the treatment that could be provided at the time. Could you tell me what sort of sanitary conditions were provided for these people from the very first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the sanitary conditions, it was a village school, and there was -- there were two toilets down by the hall, down by the sports hall, and there was a toilet with a shower. And that evening, when they were all there, I placed a table in the corridor which separated the shower with the toilet from the other part of the corridor. I did this so that the people detained there could use it, only the people kept there could use it. And the door to the shower and the toilet wasn't working; it wasn't possible to lock it. So we found a temporary solution so that it was possible to lock the door from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was it possible for you to provide those people in the school, or was it possible for you to provide the people in Mehurici with better conditions than the ones you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In Mehurici, there was just the primary school building. Mehurici is a village. There's a small police station there, but the conditions couldn't have been better than they were. The conditions were the best in that school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from the very first day who provided security for the place where the civilians were kept, and were they locked up in that sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the corridor which I had separated, there were my policemen, myself. The door to the corridor wasn't locked, but the door to the school yard was locked for security reasons, in order to make sure that no one arrived from that direction at night. I could say that we Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond were friends, in a sense, because every morning they thanked me; and if they had something to eat, they would ask me to sit down and eat with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after the first day, do you know who assumed the responsibility to feed the people who were in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that on the following day, after I had returned, and when I met -- when I saw this wounded man - I think his name was Zeljko - on the following day, I saw that the local civilian protection had already started bringing some food and other items; that they needed some blankets, et cetera. The civilian protection had already assumed the responsibility to help them; they had assumed the responsibility to ensure that sanitary conditions were adequate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long did members of your military police unit provide security for that hall? Did anyone else take over that responsibility at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we secured the hall for three, four, five days, I don't know how long exactly, and later on, the civilian police assumed the responsibility for securing it, together with the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, while you were still in Mehurici, did the Red Cross come to visit, and if so, what did they do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them on one occasion. I was in the hall at the time; I think I was even speaking to this wounded person when they said that the Red Cross had arrived. I think two women and two men entered. I went out because I thought I had nothing to do there. On the whole, they spoke to the doctor, because she was some -- because she was some sort of a chief there. I don't know what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem. Mr. Registrar, the stenographer cannot follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is that better? One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's working now. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the representatives of the Red Cross make any remarks to you, or to your command, if you are aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't say anything to me. I don't know whether they had any objections conveyed to the command, but had they, I would probably know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you spoke to this wounded man, whose name you remember as being Zeljko, did he describe the event in detail for you, or was it just simply that he said that he managed to survive the execution, as you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just told me that he survived the execution. He didn't give me any details. For me, it was sufficient that he had survived, and I was fearful as to what next, because there weren't many soldiers around and I believe to this day that I was right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This fear, was it fear for the man's life, if people knew that he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For his life, as well as the life of the others, the women, the children, and the elderly, and probably for our own lives as well, because in such an event, there would be a conflict between us and them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you include in your statement to your superior what the wounded man told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After performing your duties for four or five days, as you said, did you, Mr. HB, receive another assignment, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was fighting in that period of time in Guca Gora. I think that our people had entered Guca Gora, and I was tasked to go with several policemen, because we already knew that in Guca Gora, there was a military police unit from Zenica, that we should go and assist them, to try and protect Guca Gora, the monastery, and everything else, against looting, torturing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend on that assignment, you personally, and did you go anywhere else, and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Guca Gora for about two or three days, and after that, I went to Travnik, because there was still a chance to form this new Banja Luka brigade. And the War Presidency of Banja Luka was in Travnik. And I went there for talks, and we tried to work on the formation of such a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After taking over this new assignment, did you return to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Today, as a citizen of Sweden, when thinking about this event that you have just described to this Honourable Court, can you tell us whether this event had a permanent effect on you due to the fact that you were unable to help those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For a long time I would dream a recurrence of all those events, and I still don't know whether I could have done more. And all this time I have been suppressing this deep in my mind; however, as I look back, memories return. I'm still not sure, but I do believe that I did everything in my power.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, could you have entered the Mujahedin camp at the time and continued an investigation to see who was behind it? Was there any possibility of the army doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was simply impossible. All we could do was to compile a report, which we did. But for us to investigate, that was not possible, because we were the military police. We investigate events and actions by soldiers; however, those men were not members of our army, and we had no instructions to investigate anything. And I think that the chief of security, Hasan, sent this report to the Security Services Centre of the brigade. Now, whether anything was done, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. HB, two more brief questions. You said that those Mujahedin did not assist your battalion in any way. Tell me, did your battalion or your brigade provide any kind of assistance to those Mujahedin in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly not. We didn't even talk to them. We would only see them, speeding in a car along the road by the school and crying out in Arabic, as if they were yelling at us, because we would sometimes have a drink. Sometimes we would take a walk with some women and they didn't like this. It bothered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Did your battalion ever take part in any combat operations with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, or at least while I was there, we did not. And I don't believe that that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. HB, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I'm going to ask you some questions for the next hour or so. I want to reiterate what the Presiding Judge and my learned colleague told you earlier in the sense that if you don't understand any of my questions, I would just ask you to inform me of that and I'll rephrase or restate the question so that you do understand it. It is not my intention in any way to confuse you with the questions that I ask. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask, with the assistance of the usher, if he could perhaps move the ELMO so I could better see the witness. It's blocking my line of sight. Thank you. I would also ask if we could briefly go into private session so that we can ask the witness a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in a few moments I'm going to show you a map and ask you if you can make some markings on the map, including the routes that you took both to and from Maline on the day that you had, as you described it, that close encounter with the Mujahedin. But let me ask you first: You told us about the presence of some minefields in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you become aware of the presence of these minefields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day before our troops had left for the lines in Maline, there's a small locality, I don't know what its name is, it's on the road towards Mehurici. From the center of Mehurici, it may be a kilometre away. And there's a small bridge and a big house, which used to be some sort of a warehouse. And I think the owner of that house was Veso Balta. And there was some skirmishes there. And as the police, we arrived and we found on the bridge itself some explosives that were tied with wire to the generator, or to the battery in a car that was about a hundred metres from the bridge. One of those people, where he released the -- untied the explosive, he came across two mines, a tank mine and a trip mine, which were visible. So we didn't dare take that route because we feared for our own safety. And that is why we assumed that the area was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this bridge in the immediate area where you observed these mines, were you aware of any other minefields in the area of Maline, Bikosi or Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown a map which is, again, an enlarged version of the map we've been using throughout these proceedings. And I do have sufficient copies for everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to take a look now, if you would, please, at the map that is to your right on the projection machine. I know you can also see it in front of you, but if you could look at the paper copy of the map to your right, I would ask you if you recognise what's depicted on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to do that. If I'm right that this is the bridge in Mehurici, this here, then I think I could find my way. If somebody could tell me whether this is where the bridge in Mehurici is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, it's not really appropriate for me to tell you what's on the map. Let me first ask you if you recognise what's depicted in this map, the area that's depicted on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not too well. Not too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that it would not be helpful for us to use this map? You don't recognise of the features on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then ask you some additional questions that don't necessarily relate to the map. You told us earlier that you left the school in Mehurici between 0900 and 1000 hours, is that correct, on the day where you had the close encounter with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, not the school. I left the school in Mehurici -- I said I reached the village of Maline between 9.00 and 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What time did you leave Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might have been around 7.00, because the soldiers went in front of us. We went behind our front lines. So as the combat operations approached the village, we went behind the troops. We waited for the sign to enter the village, once the troops had captured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you wait for this sign to enter the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a small hill on the road we took. We were going on foot by the Mujahedin camp, and there's a stream there and a path which can take you to a little hill, with two big rocks, and you have a view of the whole area of Maline from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if there are any settlements or hamlets at the top of the hill where you observed Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember now. Really, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time of -- on this day, by the time you went to this hill overlooking Maline, approximately how long had you been with the 306th -- the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Do you mean all in all, or just that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All in all, sir. How long had you been with the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade on or about the 8th of June, when these events took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately five months. Five, six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the five or six months prior to this date that you were with the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, how familiar had you become with the terrain in the area around Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could say well, but only if you took the road. I know Mehurici quite well, because there's a hamlet; there are several houses behind the police station where we would go to take a bath in the stream. There's another settlement belonging to Mehurici; I think its name is Jezerci, where there were several soldiers, members of the brigade, and while I was a policeman, I would go to fetch them personally, because they didn't respond when given assignments. And above Mehurici, there's a road leading to Gluha Bukovica. Below Mehurici, you can take the road to Travnik; you turn right to go via Maline, Guca Gora, to Travnik. If you go straight ahead, you're going towards Zenica. So those would be the roads that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier today a little about the Mujahedin camp. I'd like to know if you can tell us when you first became aware that this camp was in the vicinity of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as soon as I arrived there, as soon as I arrived in Mehurici, because I would come across these people on a daily basis, driving by in cars, and they were going some place. And that is when I learned that up on the hill there was a Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, during the five or six months that you were in Mehurici, approximately how many Mujahedin were in this camp in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would wonder ourselves how many there might be. My rough estimate would be up to 150. But these people, when they put on those scarves and robes, they all look alike, so there may have been more or less of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you give us a rough estimate as to the size of the camp near Mehurici that the Mujahedin were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try, because only on two occasions did I pass by the camp; once on my way to Maline and a second time on returning, when this incident occurred. And I believe that the camp, as such, may have been 200 metres by 200 metres, so a circle with a diameter of about 200 metres. I may be wrong, I don't know, but that would be a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, you told us that this camp was approximately 200 metres from the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from the school, from the bridge in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 200, 300 metres away from the bridge. Perhaps 300 or 400 metres from the school, I really don't know. A lot of time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the day when you had the close encounter with the Mujahedin, can you tell us about your knowledge of what activities they were undertaking, if you knew anything about what they were doing from the camp near Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I knew very little. When we saw them, we saw them driving by in cars. They kept driving by in cars, going to and fro. They had a Toyota; they had some kind of a Jeep too; a van as well. They were constantly driving by in these vehicles. They would sometimes open fire. I had a girlfriend in the village, and I would sometimes go for a walk with her. And when they turned up, if she wasn't dressed according to the rules, they would open fire and they would ask that she cover herself. As to what they did, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us earlier, sir, that the -- let me ask you a couple more questions about the unit. You were assigned as the commander of a military police unit within the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us that you had, as a rough estimate, approximately 10 military policemen, but occasionally you would get older combatants who would assist you with special tasks that you were assigned; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us earlier that part of your duties included conducting investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time prior to the day on which you had the close encounter with the Mujahedin, were you or the military policemen of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade involved in any kind of investigative work concerning any activities undertaken by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you describe, sir, or how would you describe how -- or how would you characterise these Mujahedin in terms of what kind of reactions they prompted within yourself? How did you feel when you saw these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw them as foreigners, and I always asked myself what they were doing there. I don't know. We didn't have any contact, nor did we speak a common language that would enable us to communicate. I would only see such people on occasion on TV, in Arab countries or in poor countries. There were rumours according to which they had come in order to provide assistance. I don't know who they assisted. They didn't help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to the 8th of June, or thereabouts, 1993, were you afraid of these Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid, but I didn't like seeing them, because they didn't seem friendly. I don't know. Perhaps I grew up in the wrong environment. To be afraid, well, it wouldn't be the right way to put it, but I felt uneasy when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on how many occasions, if any, did you discuss the Mujahedin with the local civilian police prior to the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, did I speak about the Mujahedin with the local police? Perhaps I did, but I can't remember. But in the village, there was a cafe, and sometimes we would have coffee there and some plum brandy. A policeman and I would sometimes go there; we'd have a chat. Perhaps we discussed this on one occasion, because on one occasion the Mujahedin captured the owner of the cafe that we went to, and an inhabitant and even a combatant. But I can't really remember what happened afterwards. Something happened, but I don't know whether it was the civilian police who dealt with the matter or the civilian authorities, I really can't remember. But I know that there were problems with the owner of that cafe. Perhaps they didn't want to allow him to serve alcohol, because the cafe was close to the mosque, which is where they would go and gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall any specific instances in which you discussed any type of security concerns about the Mujahedin with any of the civilian police in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that. But the situation in the village was such that there was some individuals that the Mujahedin went after. They wanted to recruit some local inhabitants, and I think some local inhabitants were even trained in the camp. And some of the Mujahedin had wives from the village whom they had married. In that part of Mehurici, the population was divided, to a certain extent, because there were some that had religious convictions. I myself am not much of a believer, but if conflict had broken out, it would have divided the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I wasn't specifically asking about conflict, I was simply asking if you had any specific discussions with the local civilian police, in your role as commander of the military police unit, concerning the security situation with respect to this Mujahedin camp just outside Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any discussions. I don't know whether my chief of security did, because my position wasn't such that I would take those decisions. I was just the police commander. It would be the chief of security who would get involved in discussions. But as to whether he actually did this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions about the school. During the time period that you were with the military police unit of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, where did the military policemen sleep? Where did you and your military policemen sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second classroom from the right. On the ground floor, I think there were three classrooms, and we were in the middle one. In the first classroom, I think there were some people from Siprage. The members of my military police unit were in the middle classroom. And there were some members from Kotor Vares who slept classroom number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the five to six months that you were with the military police unit of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, is it your testimony that there were no Mujahedin upstairs in any of the upper floors of that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have known about that. No, they weren't up there . All the men from Siprage slept on the floor with the commander with the two toilets. I went to wash up there. They weren't up there. They weren't in the school at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the time period that you were with the military police battalion was from approximately January through June of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in response to a question from my learned colleague, you said that these persons that you initially called Arabs and then Mujahedin, you said, "In my opinion, that was an appropriate name for them," referring to the name Mujahedin. Can you tell us why you thought that was an appropriate name for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never heard of the term "Mujahedin" until the war broke out. I myself called such people Arabs. But the word "Mujahedin" means armed men, it means -- well, how would I put it, something terrible. And when I saw the way they looked, that they had those scarves and those long tunics and those beards, well, the word itself means something terrible, in my opinion. And that word is one that is very appropriate for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I'd like to turn now to the time period of approximately the 8th of June 1993, the day you when you had the close encounter with the Mujahedin. You told us that you arrived at a hill overlooking Maline sometime between 0900 and 0100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At about 9.00 or 10.00, we had already entered the village. The people had gathered in the center of the village by the hospital. There were troops of ours there. There was ongoing shooting. We were planning how to go and pass through those houses to see what was happening. We weren't sure whether there was anyone in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me take you back a little bit earlier. You told us earlier that you only passed by the Mujahedin camp on two occasions during the five- to six-month period that you were with the 306th Mountain Brigade, and the first time was that morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time you passed by that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7.00 or 8.00, half past 7.00, that was the time period. We went on foot and passed by the stream. That's the first time I found out that there was this path about the camp, and that was the quickest route to use to get to Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us also that you were on a hill overlooking Maline, waiting for a signal to enter Maline. How long did it take you to get to this hill overlooking Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps an hour or an hour and a half, because you had to be careful. There was shooting. You might come across a soldier of ours. You might not be sure whether he was one of our soldiers. But we waited there to see whether everything was safe. When we saw our troops, those troops gave us a sign and we knew that we could go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This hill that you were on waiting for that sign, were there any houses on that hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there were rocks there. I can remember these rocks. But I was only there on two occasions, 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This position that you were on, approximately how high above Maline was this location with the rocks where you were awaiting the signal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a path from Maline that leads to those rocks. There was a path that we took. As to how high it was, I don't know. Perhaps -- well, you can see Maline from that position. Perhaps 50 metres above. I don't know. I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if the location where you were awaiting the signal from your unit in Maline, do you know if that was known as Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Bikosi is a village. As far as I can remember, it's a village in the vicinity. There weren't any houses there. The place where you have these rocks was probably part of Maline. It's just a little hill, perhaps 100 metres from Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, can you then please describe your -- well, let me ask you this first: How many military policemen were with you as you entered Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10. About 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of clothing were you wearing, and what kind of arms, if any, did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had automatic weapons on us. I had an automatic rifle and a pistol. We had white insignia that said the police. We had camouflage uniforms. I don't know whether everyone had uniforms. Some, perhaps, wore jeans or jackets. But we all had white police insignia on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us, as you entered the village, what you saw with respect to the people, the civilians and any HVO soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered the village, I saw a group of women, children, and old people who were standing in front of a house. There was a yard there, too. They were standing in the road. Our troops were passing by as well, because shooting was still ongoing. I didn't know whether our troops were shooting, whether the HVO was shooting. And other people - women, children, and old people - were leaving, were coming out of their houses and asking themselves what they should do and where they should go, because among the civilians there was a lot concern. They were afraid. They kept asking if there were any Mujahedin present. They were spreading fear among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, as you arrived in the village, there was shooting that was continuing, and as this shooting was taking place, the people were coming out of their houses and gathering in the village of Maline; is that correct? Is that what you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because when I arrived there, the HVO members who had surrendered, they were standing there without their weapons. Our troops were guarding them, or they had already disarmed them. And family members probably approached them and stood by them. There were other people coming out of their houses; some of them were crying, some were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how intense the fighting and shooting was that you heard as you entered the village and saw these people gathering in front of their houses? Can you characterise the intensity of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was sporadic shooting in the village, but up in the hills, there was more intense shooting. Our troops had already set off in the direction of the hills. You could hear shooting among the houses, and one couldn't know whether fire was opened by HVO members who had remained and hadn't surrender. We didn't know whether our troops were shooting, because the village wasn't really a small one, it was quite big.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many surrendered HVO soldiers did you observe in this group when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a lot of them. There were old people, too. I don't know if they were HVO members, but there were four or five individuals in uniform, in camouflage uniforms. Perhaps I'm mistaken. Perhaps there were six or seven of them. But that's more or less the number of individuals in uniform. One person, I believe his name was Zeljko, he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately -- well, I believe you testified earlier that you remained in the village for approximately three to four hours before deciding to return to Mehurici with these people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the three to four hours that you remained in Maline, did the fighting and gunfire continue during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the gunfire continued, but it wasn't as intense. And you could even hear shells exploding. But during that three- or four-hour period, someone would open fire from a house. And since the troops was there, we would run up to the house to see what was happening, to see whether it was an HVO member shooting, to see whether someone was trying to commit a crime against the civilians. There was a lot of work to do. We only had 10 policemen. Two, three, or four policemen were standing by the civilians. Some people would be crying. You'd run to see what was happening, to see whether anyone needed any help. The situation was really difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And throughout that period, while you could still hear gunfire and even shells exploding, the people remained in front of their homes in this area, in Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then at some point in the early afternoon, you decided to take them to Mehurici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you've already told us that a small number of people were put in a truck because they were elderly or were otherwise unable to walk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you departed Mehurici with this column of individuals, the civilians and the surrendered HVO, were they in any way segregated in this column or were they co-mingled together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We all left together. There were probably family members who were present, and the families would stick together. But I believe that there were six HVO members, because we found three cases of shells in the village and we gave these shells to them so that they could carry them. There were three cases of shells. And these six went in three rows, two by two. We even spoke about certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if you know, sir, can you tell us what type of shells these were? Were these shells for an artillery weapon or for a mortar, or were they hand grenades? Or what type of shells were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe they were hand grenades, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these three cases of what you believed to be hand grenades, did the surrendered HVO soldiers have any weapons with them?
