utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the time. They had already surrendered to our army. They had surrendered before I arrived, so they had no weapons on them. But when we were forming the column, I, first of all, told everyone that it wouldn't be wise if some of them had weapons. So I said that if anyone had a weapon, they should surrender the weapons. If they found a weapon, we would have to take action. So we searched them all to make sure that they didn't have any weapons, and then we set off in the column, because there were only five policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, then, from that answer, sir, that you left the other five, approximately five, policemen in Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier, I believe, that you estimate there to be approximately 200 people in this column, including civilians and the six surrendered HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you set off in the early afternoon back towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point after you left Mehurici did any other persons join the column, whether civilians or other surrendered HVOs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. After leaving Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, after leaving Maline. I'm sorry. When you left Maline with approximately 200 people, including civilians and the six HVO soldiers, as you left Maline but before you got to the Mujahedin camp, did any other civilians or surrendered HVO soldiers join the column that you were leading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did it take this column to go from Maline to the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my judgement, two to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me take you, then, to the time you arrived by the Mujahedin camp. To the best of your recollection, approximately what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 4.00, 4.30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time you approached that camp, where were you in relation to the column of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the front of the column. I was talking to someone in the front, because the men carrying the cases with the grenades or the shells were going in front, and I was also up front. There was a policeman next to me, another one a little further away in the middle, and there was one on the other side and one at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as you approached the camp, how far away from the camp was it possible to see the camp, if you understand? As you're coming down the path, could you see the camp from a distance, or was the terrain or the vegetation such that you couldn't see the camp until you were right upon the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You couldn't see the camp, because it's a wooded area. A stream had formed a path, the water had made the path. But the camp couldn't be seen. It was full of foliage, and the vegetation was such. And then midway, where you can see, in a visible area, these two emerged who demanded that we hand them over. And on the hill, on the slope above the path, there were these three Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the two that you first encountered. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing black masks, you could only see their eyes, and camouflage uniforms. They had automatic weapons. I don't remember whether they had anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So these two individuals with black masks and camouflage uniforms, did they each have one automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I assume it was some kind of automatic rifle or long-barreled automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how far, when you first saw these two men, how far away from you -- how far away were you from them? What was the distance between you and these two men who appeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were about a metre or two near each other. At some point I thought that there were troops coming, and only when we approached, they stopped and said that they wanted to take these men. I didn't expect any such thing to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you initially believed that they were some of your troops, you say, coming? "At some point I thought that there were troops coming." You thought that they were part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see two men approaching. I didn't know who they were. I had a weapon; I held it to the ready. I thought they were normal people, our men. But as it's a bit dark there because of the leaves, and you're going down along the stream, and only once I approached they removed these socks and told me to stop. And that is when they started demanding these people. At first, I thought that there were just two of them, so I thought I could deal with them alone. And then these three appeared behind them, about five or six metres away. They just stood there and watched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if I understand what you're saying, you saw these two men and they were walking towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At first you thought they were soldiers of the ABiH, and then you saw that they were wearing masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then you said, "Only once I approached them, they removed these socks and told me to stop." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So at the time they spoke to you, they had removed the masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did they remove the masks at any point in time when you were speaking to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I assume, sir, that they were speaking to you in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did they have any type of accent that might tell you where they were from, either in Bosnia or perhaps somewhere else, or did it seem to you to be a relatively common Bosnian accent that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They simply had these masks on their heads. Whether they had an accent or not, I can't remember. But I don't think it was pure Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How much of their face could you see, given that they were wearing masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eyes, their eyes. You could see their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you see any other part of their body or skin through their clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. They had gloves with the fingers cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were having the conversation with these two men, or this discussion that you had with these two men, how far away from them were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two metres. At any point in time did you move closer to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had my weapon pointed at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, sir, how, if you were standing two metres away from this masked man, with your weapon pointed at him, he was able to put his automatic weapon into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can explain the situation to you fully. People, men, standing two metres away from me, and five metres from them, another three Mujahedin with their guns pointed at us but not saying anything. It's only these two that were talking to me. And I was holding a weapon pointed at them in one hand. And they are telling me that they want to take over care of the column, and I say to them that they can't, that I have to take the column to the school. And then they start coming out from the sides. From the thicket, other men appear. And then I turn around to look, and they approach me with weapons. I do have an automatic rifle, but they're approaching me with rifles. And as I see all these men coming out with masks, they all have their guns pointed. I could have reacted; I could have opened fire. I don't know what I would have achieved had I done that. I thought that this could be dealt with in a different way. And then they approached me and put the barrel of a rifle in my mouth, and I've already told you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I have, I would anticipate, another 15 to 20 minutes of questions for the witness, but I believe it's time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will resume work at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, right before the break, we were talking about the encounter you had right next to the Mujahedin camp in the vicinity of Mehurici. Let me ask you, sir, as the person put the automatic rifle into your mouth, where were the -- where were your fellow military policemen, and what was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was close to me. The others were as follows: One was at the back of the column, my brother was somewhere in the middle, about 10 metres away, and there was another policeman on the other side, roughly the same distance. That would be how we were distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you observe, or do you know what any of their reactions were as this soldier, or this person put this rifle into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see anything, but I did hear what their reaction was when we returned to Mehurici. When I was actually quarrelling with them, saying that I wouldn't let them take over - this was before they put the rifle in my mouth - their weapons were on the ready. However, when these others jumped out of the woods from the side, they lowered their weapons. That is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you in a moment about the persons who jumped out of the woods, but let me ask you a couple of questions about the three people standing behind the two men with the masks. You told us there were three people behind them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were those three people wearing, what type of clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform, and on that uniform, they had like a long scarf and camouflage uniforms and weapons on the ready. They were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know they were foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had beards and a different colouring. They were darker in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So those three men were not wearing any kind of mask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, as your column was approaching the Mujahedin camp - you told us earlier that the two people with the masks were walking towards you - where were those other three people? How did they come to be standing behind the two masked men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was going down the stream, the stream makes a bend, and at that bend I saw those two men first, who were approaching me. And they were perhaps some 10 metres away. So my instinct was to hold the weapon. And as I approached them, I saw these three behind them, standing there at the bend. And I got -- as I got closer, I could see them quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were the three that you saw standing at the bend also walking towards you, behind the two masked men who were walking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were walking, rather, as if they were waiting for us to approach. They were walking but slowly. They were waiting for us to come up to them, whereas the three were just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how far away were you from the two masked men when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five, six metres, maybe 10 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, sir, about the two -- the group of people that you say jumped out of the woods. Approximately how many individuals came out of the woods once the whole column had stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the column stopped, no one came out of the woods. It was after this dispute with them, whether they would take these people over or not. And as the dispute became more aggressive, and when weapons were pulled out, then these men came out. At least five of them came up there. I couldn't see beyond that, whether there were more, because by then the barrel was in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many -- excuse me. What were the people who came out of the words wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw five men who were also wearing masks and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were those five wearing the masks and the camouflage uniforms also armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how did it come to be, if you can explain to us, how the people that they took away were taken out of the column? How did that happen? How did that transpire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very hard. When these jumped out of the woods, just then this tall one came up to me and pushed his rifle into my mouth, and he forced me to turn around to see behind the column. I just know that those three cases of hand grenades had been lowered to the ground, which means they took from the column those men in uniform. And some older people picked up those cases, and even a policeman helped in carrying those cases, because when they let us go, we started running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you told us that he forced you to turn around to see behind the column, I take it at that point he had to remove the rifle from your mouth in order to allow you to turn around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. With the rifle in my mouth, I turned around and I saw that they were pointing their weapons at my brother and all the others. And they just entered into the column. And how they took people out, I don't know. They would simply put them to one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe you testified earlier, sir, that they took away 15, or perhaps as many as 20 people out of the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I was able to see. Because I counted that there were six of them in uniform, where there were others who had camouflage pants or civilians. Anyway, I think it was between 15 and maybe 20. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where were you standing when you made the assessment that 15 to 20 of them had been removed from the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was half turned towards the column to see the column. With the barrel in my mouth, I was afraid it would go off. I didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, hearing any instructions being given to the people in the column that resulted in 15 to 20 of the men being taken out of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that they simply entered and simply picked people out of the column, but I don't know, because those from the bushes, they entered among the column, they passed through the column. Now, whether they picked out individuals or what, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, though, you don't remember anyone saying anything or yelling instructions or giving instructions to the people in the column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that after these people were taken out of the column, you and the four other military police ran with the column to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They turned me around again, they took out the weapon from my mouth, and they went to one side and said that we could now proceed. And they let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you and the -- and you and your fellow military police and the column then ran in the direction of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us how far away from the Mujahedin camp this encounter took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A hundred metres. This hedge, this thicket, these woods, bordered on the camp. But it may have been about a hundred metres from the entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, approximately what time did you arrive at the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. About 5.00, 6.00, 5.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Mehurici, did you make any attempts to report what had happened to the civilian police authorities in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't see them then even, because there were a lot of people there. It was necessary to put them up. And my lip was bleeding. I had to put a bandage on it. And you had to somehow put up so many people. And once they had all entered the hall, we tried to find something to accommodate them. I was under stress. I didn't know what to do. There wasn't any command member around to whom I could complain. I just simply didn't know whom to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, when you arrived back at the Mehurici school, is it your testimony that there was no one from the 306th Mountain Brigade present in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one from the command. There were only a few policemen on duty. These older people who didn't engage in active operations, we had these elderly people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if any of the other military police who, along with you, escorted this group made any immediate report to the police, the civilian police, in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't believe so, because they would have probably addressed me first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time, sir, after this event on or about the 8th of June, 1993, did you or, to your knowledge, any of your military police lodge any kind of complaint with the civilian police authorities about what had happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When my superior, the commander, the chief of security, arrived, all of us gave a written report, which he took down, both the policemen who were there as well, and I think he sent this report to the brigade command, that is, the command of the 306th Brigade, the security service of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall the approximate day and time when you first spoke to your superior, the chief of security for the brigade, about this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was two days after the event, because he was in Zenica. And because of these operations, he couldn't get back to Mehurici as communications were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on or about the 8th of June, do you know where your brigade commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was at some forward command post. I really don't know, because I was a military policeman and he took part in the action, the operations of liberation, or whatever, that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, did you participate, or were you aware of any investigations carried out by the 306th Mountain Brigade into what happened to the people that were taken out of the column that you were escorting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know what happened to the people that were taken out of the column that you were escorting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time, but on the following day. And I set out to Maline to replace the policeman who was securing the houses in Maline. When I returned, I heard from the duty officer that some soldiers of ours, who were returning from the field, had found someone who had been wounded and they had taken him to the school. So I went to the school to make a note of this person's identity, because I was keeping a record of all the people kept in the school. And that is when I recognised this person, whose name I believe is Zeljko. I don't know why I think his name is Zeljko, but that's what I remember. I recognised him immediately, since he's the person I spoke to the most as we were at the front of the column and he was carrying one of those cases I have mentioned. He told me that he had survived an execution. The doctor was with him, the doctor who was dressing his wounds, and that is when I told him that it would be best, in my opinion, if he didn't speak about the incident to anyone. I said that when he was exchanged, he could say whatever he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me, since the Prosecution has shown you a map you couldn't comment on, at any time before 1993, did you ever go to the area of Travnik, or rather, to the area of the Bila valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Banja Luka from this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It's not far. Perhaps a hundred kilometres or more. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although, when answering questions from the Prosecution, you answered this question, I'd like to know whether, at any point in time from the time that you saw these two men who affronted you, at any point in time did one of them take these masks or stockings off their faces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did this for the sake of the transcript, because it seems as if you had said that they had taken these masks off. I don't know which line this is. It's page 60, line 16 and 17. I think that we have now clarified the interpretation of the answer you previously provided. Could you please tell me, when the column was practically stopped, you said that there were about 200 men. Were these -- 200 people. Were these people in an extended column, or was the column not that long? Was it sort of a concentrated column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know what to say. I couldn't really say whether the column had become more concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And could you clarify something else. In response to an answer to the Prosecution as to where the brigade commander was, you said that he was engaged in combat action somewhere. But could you tell me whether you knew where your battalion commander was? And did you know where the brigade commander was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The battalion commander was probably at some forward command post with the troops, and the brigade commander, well, I think that he was in Rudnik or somewhere where the brigade command was located. But I didn't have any contact with the brigade and the command. That wasn't my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One more question. You said that you gave a detailed report to your superior, and there was a written report on the investigation he conducted two days after the event. Tell me whether this was the first -- this was done on the first occasion that you could fully inform your superior about what had happened to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Because at the time he couldn't be reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. I would like to ask you a few supplementary questions on what you told us today. There have been questions about the nature of the column, whether it was a long, extended column or a concentrated one, and I've been putting these questions myself also in the past because some witnesses have told us that when they went to Mehurici, on their way they met other people who came back from Mehurici, the direction to Maline, so this might suggest that the column was quite long; and that when the first people, among them you, were confronted with the Mujahedin, not the whole group was already there. Could that be a possibility? I think you don't really know, but please tell me if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that the entire group could be seen. There was a sort of bend. As to whether everything could be seen, I don't know. I can tell you about what I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You didn't have a good view on what was happening behind you, so to speak, or beside you, because you thought you were threatened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a view of about half of the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The second question I would like to put to you is on this person you met in the music school. You told us you spoke to a person whose personal name was Zeljko, as far as you remember. You don't remember a family name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm not even sure that Zeljko is his name. But that's what I remember. I seem to remember his name being Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And he was a witness to the events in Bikosi, and he was found a day later in the field by your soldiers, or by someone else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that's how it was. I heard that our troops had found him and taken him to the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Another point in his witness statement, in his statement before this Court, is that he said he was transported from Maline to Mehurici in a car and was not a member of the -- in the walking column to Mehurici. Do you have any explanation for that, or would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Some people, a number of people who had already been wounded, who had been wounded before I reached the civilians, a group was transported in a vehicle from Maline. Later I found out that the doctor was there, too. I wasn't present, but some of the soldiers or the commanders who entered the village must have done that before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let's go to another matter and to another witness who has testified before this Court. This is a written statement that we have received in evidence in July. It's under seal also. This witness is describing the following event. He is in a column that has been stopped, and he is one of the persons that has been taken to Bikosi, among other people. And what he says about the meeting with the Mujahedin is the following: "Approximately half of them were Mujahedins and the other half were local Muslims." Is that your impression also, or could you tell -- could you not tell this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say because the people were masked. As to whether they were locals, as to the reason for which they had masks on them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This witness, incidentally, is also one of the witnesses who said, "while we were escorted, we saw a different group coming from another direction," escorted by these people. What matters to me is the following, what he said: "I can recall that all of them," and he means the Mujahedin and the local Muslim, "I can recall that all of them had insignia with some green and black on it." Is that also your recollection, or didn't you see anything like it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And he said also the following: "Three or four of the Muslim soldiers had a mask on their face, mostly green or black. Those with the masks were Bosnian soldiers. I was able to tell that when I heard them talking." My question is the following: "Three or four of the Muslim soldiers had a mask on their face, mostly green or black." Do you remember these colours, green or black masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Black ones. The men standing in front of me were wearing black masks. You could only see their eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Other people have also talked about ribbons around their hats. Do you have any recollection about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were some sort of ribbons, and there was some sort of an inscription on these ribbons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you read the inscription of those ribbons? Was there a text on it or a particular ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was something inscribed on them. They were wearing them on -- around their foreheads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If there was something inscribed on it, on them, could you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was some sort of Arabic script. It wasn't in our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My last question is related to what another witness said in his statement to this Court. He is describing the situation in Maline in his statement, so at the very beginning of the day -- of the 8th of June. He said the following: "I went with a BH army soldier to another house, and he asked me whether there were any weapons in the house and I showed him a hunting rifle. He hung it over his shoulder and ordered me to lock the house. My wife was in the house at the time and she asked where they were going to take us, and the soldier said they would take us to Mehurici so that the Mujahedin would not kill us." Could you explain to me this story? The fact that the Mujahedin were somewhere in the neighbourhood of Mehurici, was that a fact the Croats came up with that made them scared, or was it something you took into account already before going to Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that event. This isn't something I have referred to. I don't remember such an event. But there was fear of such events. People were afraid that such forces might commit certain acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me put to you a related question. Before you went to Maline, before the evacuation took place, was there already an idea among your police force, or in the army itself, to evacuate the persons from Maline.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, no, because I think that the command didn't want to go further than Maline. But as there was ongoing fighting there, I did this on my own initiative, because the command wanted me to protect the civilians. While there was fighting, I couldn't protect these people, so -- I couldn't protect these people in the village, so I decided to protect them in Mehurici. And I did this on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you also mentioned this morning that one of your motives was that they could be exchanged against other prisoners taken by the HVO, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So how does this square, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because I had already heard about this system of exchange. When they'd already arrived in the school, I heard about the system of exchange. I heard about this from the people who were in the school. That's the first time that I found out that the civilian population would be exchanged for HVO members and for BH army members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This is something different from what you told us this morning, I guess, but I'm not sure I have a remembrance of what you were saying, that the exchange of prisoners was one of your motives for taking them away from Maline. But I'm not able to check it. My last question, then: It has already been alluded to by others this morning, I think, and let me question you -- let me put the question more squarely to you. Are you familiar with the fact that in April of the same year, so let's say two months before these events, people were killed by the Mujahedin in the neighbourhood of Mehurici, or are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You heard the full story, or only some accidental remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it was in April that I heard about it. We were guarding some positions when we returned. I think it was when the Mujahedin captured and took to prison -- took away to prison the owner of the cafe. Well, on that occasion, there was a rumour, according to which they had killed someone in a Croatian village, I think. But I really don't know whom they killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Is that all you know about the previous incidents with the Mujahedin, the cafe holder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only incident that I witnessed. And it was only when we returned to Mehurici that I heard that they had taken this person, Alija, away and some other people as well, because they served alcohol. But later on these people were released. I don't know anything about other incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that in the month of April some five or six people were killed in Miletici as a result of military action by the Mujahedin in Poljanice? That is an unknown story to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have two very short questions. When you went from Mehurici to Maline, when you went to Maline in the morning, did you have an order to go there, and who gave you the order to go to Maline with men from your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the brigade command told me that if the action was successful, if our troops were able to reach Maline, I should protect the civilians and their property with my men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in Maline, the column that was taken to Mehurici, was this something you did on your own initiative, or were you carrying out a specific order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my personal initiative. And my order was to protect the civilians, and I thought that I couldn't do this with 10 men, because the village is a big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To protect them. But to protect them from whom, from what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was afraid, because there was fighting, there was shooting, and I was afraid that the men from the camp, the Mujahedin, might reach those people in the village. That was what I was afraid of. And I think that the command also had this in mind, and that is why they sent the police there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your mind, when the attack on Maline took place, did the Mujahedin participate in the attack, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why did you think the Mujahedin might go to Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, do you know why? Because in my assessment, they were vultures of a kind. They would engage in looting. They would go to those villages. After combat, I was afraid that they might camp, and I thought that that camp near Mehurici might pose a threat. Maybe I was mistaken, but my order was to protect the civilians, and in my opinion, I acted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have, sir, just a couple of questions in follow-up with those questions put to you by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you were afraid of the Mujahedin reaching the people in Maline, why did you take that column consisting of those 200 civilians within a hundred yards of their camp, on the outskirts of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I thought that they couldn't seize men from us, from the Bosnian army, from the police, because we passed along that route going to Maline. We passed by the camp and nothing was happening; we didn't see anything. We felt that we could pass by. However, things happened differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you went to Maline to protect the civilians from the Mujahedin, I suggest to you that it was not a reasonable step for you to take to take those very people that you were sent to protect from the Mujahedin right past the Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That route was taken by civilians, by our troops, and I -- we never had any conflict with them. To the extent of armed exchanges, there had been no clashes. So I thought that if the police was escorting the people, that none of them would do anything. That was the only and shortest route for us to reach Mehurici. I did not expect them to seize those men from us, because that hadn't happened until then. They could have come in the dark, and with 10 men, I cannot watch over the whole village. They could have come under cover of darkness. And I thought that the best idea would be to take them all together and to guard them and to save their lives. However, what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you were describing you were assigned to the village after combat operations, was that assignment to protect the civilian population living in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand that assignment, or rather, how did you understand it? Was it protection against all dangers that accompany combat operations, including the possible appearance of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With a group of 10 men in a large village, was it possible to protect those people from all the risks entailed when the front line is nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still believe that I couldn't protect them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering some questions before about this protection, you said that when you saw the villagers, they were in different moods; some of them were afraid, some were crying, and some were asking you whether there were any Mujahedin around. This reaction of the civilian population, did it make you have second thoughts about leaving the villagers in the village, if they were so afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: His Honour asked you a question about exchanges. I will remind you that on page 26, lines 21 to 25, and on page 27, lines 1 to 3, you described your conversation with the Mujahedin who intercepted you. And as it says in this line, you said: "I told them that it was not possible for them to take those men," that you were members of the army and that you have to take the whole column to the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You then said that there was a possibility of an exchange. This exchange that you mentioned, in answer to one of the questions, and that you referred to when talking to the Mujahedin, was that actually an attempt to persuade the Mujahedin to let you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question linked to your knowledge about this event in Miletici; this was April, or end of April, 1993. You said that you were on some front lines. Could you tell me where the 1st Battalion was stationed, which lines, and how far were they from Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the names of those villages are. It was a long time ago. But I know that quite a way from Bila, from a mine, you went through a wood, near a stream, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this linked to any -- well, not significant, I can't call it significant when criminals are involved. Were they defensive actions linked to a terrible event that occurred in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly. I think we were there for four or five days, holding our positions. We were in trenches. There was no fighting. We were just holding on to our positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, just one question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answer to a question from the President, you said that you received your order from the brigade command. You said that should our troops succeed in Maline, that you should go there. You used that expression,"our troops," a few other times. When using that expression, you were referring to members of the 306th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, you have just completed your testimony. Thank you for coming to The Hague and for contributing to the establishment of the truth by the answers you gave to all the questions put to you. I wish you a safe journey home, and best wishes for the future. I will adjourn the hearing immediately because we have overstepped our time limit by 10 minutes. I thank all the participants, and I invite you to come back here for the hearing beginning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
